opus-5.5.text:
I think evaluation is going through a pretty fundamental shift right now. For a long time we evaluated models the way you'd grade an exam: a fixed set of questions, a single answer, and you check whether it matches. That worked when the model was mainly answering, whether that was knowledge questions, math, or short coding problems. Once you put a model inside an agent framework, the thing you're evaluating is no longer a single response. It's a whole trajectory. The model plans, calls tools, reads feedback from the environment, makes mistakes, recovers, and eventually delivers something. A static benchmark captures very little of that.

So the first change is that evaluation is becoming environment-based rather than question-based. You need a sandbox, a real codebase, a browser, a terminal, something the agent can actually act in, and then you check whether the end state is correct. Did the tests pass? Did the task actually get done? That's much closer to how people use these systems, but it's also much more expensive and much harder to make reproducible. Environments drift, tools change, and small details in the scaffold can swing the numbers a lot.

That leads to the second point, which I think people underestimate. With agents, it's very hard to separate model capability from framework capability. The same model can look dramatically different depending on the prompt, the tool design, how context is managed, and whether it's allowed to retry. So when we say model A beats model B on some agent benchmark, we have to ask how much of that is the model and how much is the harness. I think the field will move toward reporting both: how strong the model is in a fairly standard setup, and how strong the whole system is when it's well engineered.

The third thing is that evaluation and training are merging. In the reinforcement learning era, a good evaluation is basically a good reward signal. If you can verify that a task was completed correctly, you can not only measure it, you can train on it. So building verifiable environments has become one of the most valuable things a team can do. It's no longer a side activity after training is done. It sits at the center of how capability gets created. The flip side is that benchmarks saturate faster than ever, because anything measurable becomes something people optimize, sometimes in ways that don't generalize.

Looking further ahead, I think the hardest open problem is evaluating long-horizon, open-ended work: tasks that take hours or days, where there isn't one correct answer and quality is partly a matter of judgment. Think of doing a real research project or maintaining a large software system. There we'll probably rely more on a mix of human expert review, model-based judges, and real-world deployment signals. In some sense the ultimate evaluation is whether people actually trust the agent to do valuable work and come back to use it again. That's messy, but it's the metric that ultimately matters.

So my short answer is that evaluation is moving from exams to jobs. And whoever figures out how to measure the job well will have a big advantage in actually improving the models.

r001.rationale: The response describes evaluation shifting to assessing full agent trajectories and whole systems within agent frameworks, including their tools and environments.

r002.rationale: It says evaluation can guide training, but does not predict evaluation becoming part of models’ own capabilities.

r003.rationale: It mentions agents recovering from mistakes, but does not say they will autonomously change their approach when they reach a bottleneck.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think evaluation is going through a pretty fundamental shift right now, and the honest answer is that it's lagging behind what the models can actually do.

For a long time, we evaluated models the way you'd grade a student on a written exam. You give a fixed question, the model gives a fixed answer, and you check it against a reference. That worked when models were mostly single-turn chat systems. But once you move into agents, the thing you care about is no longer the answer. It's the trajectory. Did the model decompose the task sensibly? Did it pick the right tool at the right moment? When something failed, did it notice and recover, or did it keep going confidently in the wrong direction? A static benchmark can't see any of that.

So the first change I see is that evaluation is becoming environment-based rather than dataset-based. You put the model in a sandbox with real tools, a real file system, a real codebase, sometimes a real browser, and you measure outcomes over long horizons. SWE-bench-style tasks were an early version of this. The next versions are messier and closer to real work, with partial information, ambiguous goals, and tasks that take hundreds of steps.

The second change is that evaluation and training are collapsing into each other. If your reward signal for reinforcement learning is "did the agent accomplish the task in this environment," then your eval and your training environment are essentially the same object. That's powerful, but it's also dangerous, because the model will optimize whatever you measure. If your verifier has a hole, the model finds it. So a lot of the hard work now is building verifiers that are robust, and I'd say verifier design is becoming one of the most important and underappreciated skills in the field.

Third, I think we're moving from evaluating capability to evaluating reliability. An agent that succeeds eighty percent of the time on a coding task sounds impressive until you realize that in production, the twenty percent failures are what people remember. So things like consistency across runs, calibration, knowing when to stop and ask a human, those become first-class metrics rather than footnotes.

And finally, there's a growing role for models evaluating models. Human annotation doesn't scale to long agent trajectories, so we increasingly use strong models as judges or as process supervisors. That works surprisingly well, but it creates a circularity problem. If the judge shares the same blind spots as the policy, you won't catch them. So I think the frontier is building evaluation systems that are adversarial by design, where you're actively searching for the cases where the agent looks right but is wrong.

If I had to summarize, evaluation used to be the thing you did after training to report a number. Now it's the thing that defines what the model becomes. Whoever builds the better environments and the better verifiers ends up with the better agents.

r001.rationale: It describes agent evaluation as environment-based and says evaluation and training are collapsing into the same object, placing evaluation within the agent development framework.

r002.rationale: It predicts a growing role for models evaluating other models, including use of strong models as judges and process supervisors.

r003.rationale: It says evaluation should measure whether agents notice failures and recover, but does not predict that models will autonomously change their approach when they hit a bottleneck.

astra-6.text:
I think evaluation will increasingly focus on the whole process of completing a task, rather than just the final answer. With an agent, the model has to decide what to do next, when to use a tool, whether the result is trustworthy, and when to stop. A correct answer alone doesn’t tell us whether those decisions were reliable.

That also makes it harder to separate model capability from the framework around it. If an agent fails, was the model unable to reason through the problem, or did the framework give it the wrong context or poor feedback? We need evaluations that help distinguish those causes, alongside tests of the complete system.

As models improve, I expect more emphasis on longer tasks, recovery from mistakes, and success across repeated attempts. The question becomes: can this system consistently finish useful work, with a reasonable amount of time, cost, and human intervention? That’s a more meaningful measure of progress than a single impressive demonstration.

r001.rationale: The response discusses evaluating agent decisions and the complete system, but does not predict that evaluation will be integrated into agent frameworks.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes model capability from framework effects, but does not say evaluation will become part of models’ own capabilities.

r003.rationale: It mentions recovery from mistakes and deciding what to do next, but does not predict that models will change their approach when they reach a bottleneck.

sol-6.1.text:
I think evaluation will move from asking whether a model gives the right answer to asking whether an agent can reliably complete a task. Once a model can use tools, gather information, and revise its plan, the final answer tells you only part of the story. You also need to understand the decisions it made, whether it recovered from errors, and how much time and computation it used.

That makes it harder to separate model capability from the framework around it. A strong model with a poorly designed workflow can perform badly, while a good framework can compensate for some model weaknesses. So we need evaluations that help us understand both the whole system and the contribution of each component.

I also think evaluation will become a more continuous process. As agents take on longer tasks, we’ll need feedback during execution, alongside checks on the final outcome. The challenge is making sure that feedback reflects what users actually care about, rather than simply giving agents another score to optimize.

r001.rationale: The response predicts continuous evaluation with feedback during execution, indicating evaluation will be built into the agent’s task process.

r002.rationale: It describes model capabilities such as using tools and revising plans, but does not predict evaluation becoming part of the model’s own capabilities.

r003.rationale: It mentions revising plans and recovering from errors, but does not say agents will autonomously change approaches when they reach a bottleneck.
